none: Translation of the sūrah only; no commentary point.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning concerns those who want only worldly life and deny the Hereafter; lawful enjoyment of this world can also apply to believers.
rows.anchor: it is understood here to refer to those who desire this life only and deny the reality of the Hereafter (R)

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some read the promise as God hastening believers’ reward for righteous aims in this world without reducing their Hereafter reward.
rows.anchor: God would “hasten” their reward in this world without decreasing it in the Hereafter (Q)

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: One reported occasion is that the verse concerned believers in the Prophet’s time whose religious acts were driven by ostentation.
rows.anchor: revealed about certain believers during the time of the Prophet who were given to religious ostentation in their actions (see also 107:6; Aj)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nullification of actions performed with wrong intentions in the Hereafter is also discussed at 3:22.
rows.anchor: For the manner in which actions with the wrong intentions are rendered null in the Hereafter, see 3:22c

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some invoke the hadith that actions are judged according to intentions in explaining the fate of deeds.
rows.anchor: Some mention in this connection the famous ḥadīth, “Verily actions are [judged] according to [their] intentions” (Q)

rows.speaker: IK, Z
rows.claim: One report names Noah’s son who stayed behind Yām.
rows.anchor: to have been named Yām (IK, Z)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Another reported name for Noah’s son is Kanʿān.
rows.anchor: Yām (IK, Z) or Kanʿān (Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spiritually, the mountain represents the false security, stability, and permanence that deniers of God assign to the world.
rows.anchor: false sense of security, stability, and permanence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to remain steadfast is addressed to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: Be steadfast, a command addressed to the Prophet

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some interpret steadfastness as holding firmly to the Quran.
rows.anchor: understood by some to mean that he should hold steadfastly to the Quran (R)

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The command extends to those who repent alongside the Prophet, identified here as his Companions.
rows.anchor: it is a command also directed toward those who turn in repentance along with him, namely, the Prophet’s Companions (Q)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The prohibition on inclining toward wrongdoers means believers must not approve the Makkan idolaters’ actions.
rows.anchor: incline not toward the wrongdoers means that the believers should never approve of the actions of the Makkan idolaters (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prayers named here are generally understood as the five canonical daily prayers.
rows.anchor: The prayers here are usually understood as referring

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One identification of the two day-end prayers is dawn and sunset.
rows.anchor: the prayers at the two ends of the day are interpreted to be the prayers performed at dawn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another identification of the two day-end prayers is dawn and late afternoon.
rows.anchor: or at dawn and in the late afternoon

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third identification is midday and late afternoon.
rows.anchor: A similar range of opinion regarding the five prayers can be seen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The early-night prayers may collectively mean sunset and night prayers.
rows.anchor: the early hours of the night can collectively refer to the prayers performed at sunset and during the night

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the early-night phrase may refer only to the night prayer.
rows.anchor: or to the latter only (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The range of interpretations of the five prayers resembles the disagreement over which prayer is the middlemost at 2:238.
rows.anchor: A similar range of opinion regarding the five prayers can be seen in identifying the middlemost prayer in 2:238

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The daily prayers expiate minor sins committed between them, provided major sins are avoided.
rows.anchor: the Prophet is reported to have said, “Verily from prayer to prayer there is an expiation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: More generally, the positive effects of good deeds can counterbalance the negative effects of evil deeds.
rows.anchor: In a more general sense, it can refer to the manner in which the positive effects of good actions can offset the negative effects of evil actions

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet teaches that a good deed following an evil deed erases it.
rows.anchor: Follow up an evil deed with a good deed

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The heart is polished by remembrance of God; prayer and remembrance can affect a heart darkened by sin.
rows.anchor: In a ḥadīth the Prophet said, “For everything there is a polish, and the polish of the heart is the remembrance of God”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The link between patience and God’s reward is discussed in the commentary on 11:11.
rows.anchor: On the connection between patience and God’s reward, see v. 11c

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other verses also promise that God will not neglect believers’ reward: 3:171, 7:170, 9:120, 12:56, 12:90, and 18:30.
rows.anchor: Other verses that mention how God will not neglect the reward of believers include 3:171; 7:170; 9:120; 12:56, 90; 18:30

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph is the third of six sūrahs whose openings contain alif, lām, rāʾ and speak of the Book.
rows.anchor: opening verses include the letters alif, lām, and rāʾ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah belongs to the Makkan period.
rows.anchor: Yūsuf belongs to the Makkan period

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah recounts Joseph’s life in the Quran’s longest and most continuous single narrative.
rows.anchor: constitutes the longest and most continuous single narrative in the Quran (vv. 3–101)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quranic outline corresponds broadly to Genesis 37:1–46:7, though the accounts differ significantly.
rows.anchor: corresponds to Genesis 37:1–46:7, although there are several significant differences between the Quranic and Biblical accounts

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: A report says the story was revealed after Jewish scholars persuaded Makkan idolaters to ask Muhammad about Joseph’s life and legacy.
rows.anchor: Makkan idolaters to ask the Prophet about certain details pertaining to Joseph’s life and legacy (R)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Another report says the story was revealed after the Prophet’s Companions asked him to tell them a story.
rows.anchor: God revealed the story of Joseph to the Prophet after his Companions had asked him to provide them with a story (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph tells Jacob of his special dream; Jacob warns him not to tell his jealous brothers, who plot against him and cast him into a well.
rows.anchor: Joseph discloses a special dream he had to his father, Jacob, who warns Joseph not to convey his dream to his brothers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A caravan rescues Joseph, and an Egyptian high official buys him; the official is identified with the Biblical Potiphar.
rows.anchor: purchased in Egypt by a high-ranking official (v. 21), identified with the Biblical figure Potiphar

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Potiphar’s unnamed wife, Zulaykhā, falls in love with Joseph and tries to seduce him, but he resists.
rows.anchor: Zulaykhā (not mentioned by name), falls in love with him and attempts to seduce him, but Joseph does not succumb

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After false accusations and widespread rumors about the incident, Joseph is imprisoned.
rows.anchor: After false accusations before Potiphar (v. 25) and widespread rumors throughout Egypt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph is later cleared, released from prison, and appointed to high office in Egyptian society.
rows.anchor: Joseph is later exonerated, released from prison, and appointed to high office in Egyptian society

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s parents and brothers eventually join him in Egypt, fulfilling the dream from the beginning of the story.
rows.anchor: the dream he had at the beginning of the story is fulfilled (v. 100)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s story has inspired a remarkable range of artistic, literary, and spiritual works in Islamic tradition.
rows.anchor: has supplied material for an astonishing array of artistic, literary, and spiritual works in the Islamic tradition

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islamic literature associates Joseph’s exceptional beauty with Divine Beauty, patience in adversity, and dream interpretation.
rows.anchor: exceptional physical beauty, is often associated in Islamic literature with the reflection of Divine Beauty, patience in times of adversity, and the art of dream interpretation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentaries on the sūrah draw on a rich tradition that includes folkloric and imaginative material.
rows.anchor: The commentaries on this sūrah reflect this rich tradition and incorporate into their accounts material that is often folkloric and imaginative

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The episode involving Joseph and Zulaykhā inspired many mystical and literary romances.
rows.anchor: a variety of mystical and literary romances

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One especially well-known romance is Jāmī’s Persian poem Joseph and Zulaykhā; Jāmī lived from 898/1492.
rows.anchor: a lengthy Persian poem entitled

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Suhrawardī uses motifs from the story in a philosophical treatise to explain love’s metaphysical meaning and its relation to beauty, joy, sadness, and longing.
rows.anchor: uses the motifs and symbols from the story of Joseph in his philosophical treatise On the Reality of Love

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many interpret the story spiritually as the human soul’s separation from its Divine Origin and its return.
rows.anchor: Many interpret the story of Joseph symbolically and spiritually as an account of the separation of the human soul from its Divine Origin and its return to It

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At its highest level, the story is read as a love tale between the human lover and the Divine Beloved.
rows.anchor: it has often been seen as an exalted love tale that speaks about the relationship between the human lover and the Divine Beloved

rows.speaker: al-Maybudī
rows.claim: Al-Maybudī describes the story as lovers’ separation and union, inviting the wounded and lovers to contemplate love’s pain and longing.
rows.anchor: al-Maybudī says in his Quran commentary, “How beautiful the story of Joseph is!
